analysis: Brokskat makkii chah combines the widespread regional makai maize term and Purik chah (explicitly identified by SchmidtKaulp248). Printed punctuation must establish alternatives versus compound. Neither is a secure inherited reflex of markaka the bird; do not use the surprising DB bird etymology as an accent baseline.

Brokskat byɨɨ is recorded for man and son, but neither dāraka nor putra supplies an obvious segmental route. Its kin/person polysemy and unusual vowel notation require primary Brokskat lexical evidence; retain it as a replacement pending etymology.

Brokskat bede many may be related to grown/big or a regional bahu derivative, but the dental and vowel sequence do not choose between vivr̥ddha and bahura. Initial stress is retained while the immediate input remains unresolved.

Ushojo marxoor markhor is the Persian compound mār-khōr snake-eater animal name, rather than an inherited śarabha deer reflex. Initial survey stress belongs to the adapted compound and supplies no old Indo-Aryan accent test.

SchmidtKaul2008p247 lists thoktse mattock (tentatively), dzen milk, samdalmo moustache and ziṅgat neck as Purik loans. They are lexical replacements alongside inherited alternatives, not failures of spʰiya, dugdha, phuṅga or grīvā sound laws.

Ushojo mootha(a)ro mirror may contain face/mouth plus a seeing or holding element, but neither compound structure nor source is secure. Final/medial stress is recorded without constructing a Sanskrit ancestor from the English meaning.

Ushojo šaadu monkey does not preserve the consonants of vānara or markaṭa. A regional śādu/sādu monkey term, perhaps transferred or borrowed, needs lexical confirmation; final stress remains unexplained historically.

Brokskat cwalto morning is distinct from Ushojo loceki and cannot be derived from ruṣṭa by gloss identity. A dawn/time adverb with final to morphology is possible, but its initial stress has no secure ancestral comparison.
Ushojo caṭu mortar resembles regional caṭṭu container/tool vocabulary, not kapāla. Retain final stress and investigate a local vessel term rather than imposing a skull/cup etymology.

Ushojo cical / xata mud has two forms. cical matches the kicca/cical mud family with additional l; xata may be a separate soil/filth word. Split them before counting cognacy or treating two stress marks as a single accent conflict.

Brokskat stored mateds mulberry is a candidate for the madhura-vr̥kṣa/matoc̣ regional mulberry formation, but the printed consonants and stress must be recovered before accepting it. A superficial match to muṭṭa tree is insufficient.

Brokskat stored nto name is likely a faulty reading of the source vowel sequence in the nāman/name set, but the exact scan must decide. Do not reconstruct a consonant cluster or assign a research link from presumed OCR correction alone.

Ushojo neero near resembles a contracted nikaṭa/nēṛa regional near formation, but deletion of k/ṭ and absence of a flap need demonstration. Initial stress on long ee is secure as transcribed; ancestry remains provisional.

Brokskat kunjaa nineteen differs from Ushojo anbiš/ūnaviṁśati. An alternative subtractive expression or Tibetan-related numeral formation is possible; the printed item and other teen numerals must be compared before deriving the first element from ūna.

Ushojo dege cer bi ninety and poẓ bi hundred are renewed arithmetic expressions involving ten plus four twenties and five twenties. Their components can be compared with daśa, catvāraḥ, pañca and viṁśati, but whole expressions are not direct navati/śata reflexes and must be counted as compounds.
Ushojo aṛdez noon is a plausible half-day compound with ardha and day/divasa. Final stress is a compound result; source and segmental confirmation are required before accepting both component links.

Brokskat stored nurs not has an implausible r compared with the numeral nine nur and may reflect OCR of a vowel/nasal mark plus negative morphology. The printed form must be read before assigning ná or naiva.

Ushojo guŋge owl appears to be a regional/expressive bird name; no regular connection to ulūka is established. Final stress and the velar/nasal sequence remain documented without a manufactured old accent.
Ushojo tothi parrot is a regional tota/toti-type bird name rather than śuka. It may be borrowed or expressive; its initial stress cannot be evaluated as inherited śúka accent.

Ushojo iṭhil pestle is unrelated in visible segments to músala. A pounder/tool derivative is possible, but the initial glottal stop and final il need an independently identified root; final stress remains a source observation.

Ushojo jakulege pinch (past) contains apparent kul/uleg verbal morphology and stresses the later stem/suffix. Identify the present and causative paradigm before comparing it with an old lexical root; no secure etymon is assigned.

Ushojo ṣiṣo pine cone may be a head-shaped metaphor from the head word or a distinct conifer term. A śīrṣa metaphor is plausible but not demonstrated by a single gloss; do not count it as an inherited head reflex without semantic evidence.

Ushojo alica plum is the regional alūča-type fruit name with final stress; contact transmission is more plausible than direct accent inheritance from a selected Sanskrit plum noun. Exact donor and vowel adaptation remain open.

Brokskat anar pomegranate is the Persian anār fruit name, replacing inherited dāḍima/daṇu forms. Its final stress is a loan-adaptation outcome and cannot explain or contradict the inherited dāḍima accent set.

Brokskat phaltsaa poplar does not segmentally continue śiṁśapā. A local Tibetan/Purik tree term is plausible but not explicitly established in the source loan list consulted; retain an unresolved regional replacement.
